newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka teams up with Europe against paedophiles.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka teams up with Europe against paedophiles.

text.p: Swiss police are expected in Sri Lanka next week to track down victims of an alleged Swiss child abuser, marking a new era of international cooperation in the fight against paedophilia, police said on Wednesday.
The Swiss are expected to record statements from victims to be used for his proscecution back home, Noel Francis, assistant superintendent of the police crimes division, told Reuters.

The visit by the Swiss comes a week after a team of Dutch police officals visited this tropical Indian Ocean island on the trail of a Dutch investor who is believed to have abused at least eight young boys.
Victims told investigators the 50-year-old man videotaped and photographed them performing sexual acts and identified seaside hotels which were used for the purpose, Francis said.

"Here is a case where law enforcement agencies in the abuser's country and the country of the victim have helped each other to bring evidence together," said a lawyer who appears on behalf of victims, mostly children from poor families living along the island's western and southern coastal belt.
"It is encouraging to us in that some day, we may be the ones asking these countries for help," he said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Human rights groups say poverty-stricken Sri Lanka, which relies on tourism as a main source of foreign exchange and employment, has become a popular destination for paedophiles worldwide.

Sri Lanka passed tough laws in 1995 aimed at discouraging foreign paedophiles. They call for a minimum five years' jail and maximum 20 years for pimps and their clients. The laws push the age of consent up to 18 for boys and 16 for girls, making sex with anyone under this age a crime.
Child abuse cases are pending against two Swiss, a German and a Belgian national in Sri Lankan courts. Another Swiss, who jumped bail, is being tried in absentia.
But some activists blame authorities for dragging their feet on investigations.

"Police are not taking enough interest," said Kalyananda Tiranagama of Lawyers for Human Rights and Development, a non-governmental organisation. "We're not at all satisfied with the way investigations are being carried out."
Tiranagama said police needed to go deeper into cases, instead of merely arresting suspects and filing charges.
"We want them to investigate hotels which cater to these activities, go after local pimps and after parents who allow their children to get involved with paedophiles," he said.
